title: GLial IMMunE Response in pediatric ME/CFS
summary:
As the initiators of this study, our primary interest is in deepening our understanding of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) in children and adolescents. In particular, we aim to better understand the disease-related changes in physiological functions and processes associated with ME/CFS. To date, there is no specific laboratory value or clear measurement parameter that allows for a definitive diagnosis of this condition. Therefore, one of the study’s goals is to identify key factors associated with the onset of symptoms—particularly cognitive symptoms. To do this, we are using a method that allows us to transform certain immune cells from the blood (monocytes) so that they resemble the brain’s immune cells, the microglia. In this way, we hope to identify key processes that could cause inflammation in the brain. Our goal is to better understand why cognitive symptoms arise and, ideally, to identify potential approaches for providing targeted help to those affected in the future.

The goal of this study is therefore to better understand which biological mechanisms contribute to the onset and progression of ME/CFS in children and adolescents—with a particular focus on cognitive symptoms. The planned blood draw will allow us to examine blood cells directly. In addition, there is the possibility that the Mo

In addition, there is a possibility that monocytes—which are immune cells in the blood—can transform into microglia-like cells under certain conditions. Microglia are the brain’s immune cells. By studying them, we hope to gain new insights into the role of the immune system in ME/CFS, particularly as it relates to the brain.
To answer these questions, an additional 23 ml of blood will be collected for the study during a blood draw that is already scheduled as part of routine care. This additional amount poses no health risk. The blood will be used to analyze the immune cells and examine their behavior in the laboratory.
In order to interpret the results correctly, we need comparative data from children and adolescents who do not have ME/CFS. These individuals form what is known as the control group. By comparing the two groups, we hope to better identify disease-specific changes.
To achieve this goal, a collaboration has been established between the University Clinic for Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine at the OWL University Hospital of Bielefeld, the on-site University Outpatient Clinic for Post-Acute Infection Syndromes (PAIS), Post-COVID, and ME/CFS, and the “Anatomy and Cell Biology” research group at the Bielefeld Medical School.
The scientific findings could pave the way for new therapeutic approaches in the long term. In particular, this could lead to improved medical options in the future for affected children and adolescents, for whom treatment options are currently limited.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patient group:
Inclusion criteria:
●    Age 12–17 years at the time of sample collection
●    Presence of medically diagnosed ME/CFS based on the Canadian Consensus Criteria and current national and international diagnostic guidelines [37].
●    Moderate or severe severity (Bell score of at least 10 and no more than 50)

Control group:
Inclusion criteria:
●    Aged 12–17 years at the time of sample collection
●    Elective pediatric surgical procedure at the Bethel Children’s Center
Exclusion criteria:
Patient group:
Exclusion criteria:
●    Presence of other pre-existing neurological, psychiatric, immunological, or rheumatological conditions prior to the onset of ME/CFS
●    Acute infection at the time of presentation

Control group:
Exclusion criteria:
●	Pre-existing neurological, psychiatric, immunological, or rheumatological conditions
●    Current or past ME/CFS, post-COVID syndrome, or PAIS in the patient or first-degree relatives
●    Acute infection at the time of presentation
